name: Earn Trust
definition: Leaders listen attentively, speak candidly, and treat others respectfully. They are vocally self-critical, even when doing so is awkward or embarrassing. They do not believe they, or their team, smell like roses. They benchmark themselves and their teams against the best.
why: Trust is hard to earn and easy to lose. You earn it by making a hard promise and keeping it. Customers give you the benefit of the doubt on the next thing because the last thing arrived as advertised. The same rule holds inside the company. People stop spending cycles on politics when they believe you will do what you said, and that you will say the thing that is true even when it is about you.

Look for vocal self-criticism that is about the work, not a performance. Leading with the miss is how you get help. Projecting an illusion of perfection is exhausting, and it makes other people hide their own problems. Vocally self-critical is not throwing your team under the bus, and it is not fishing for sympathy. It is naming your part, fixing it, and making the lesson usable by someone else.

Earn Trust also means you listen to critics, you argue for the customer, and you treat people with dignity. You judge the work and the data, not motives. You give credit when another team carried the thing. You do not paint lines on the turf. Territorialism is expensive. Humility is cheaper, and it is how you find the blind spot you cannot see from inside your own story.

When someone tells you that you broke trust, the first move is not a defense. The first move is to earn it back. Competence is part of that. People trust you because you are good at the work, not because you are pleasant in the hallway.
calibrationIntro: Score candor, respect, and vocal self-criticism. Skip examples that are really about delegation, networking, or delivery theater. Under hides, blames, or performs perfection. Over performs humility, people-pleases, or burns the team in public.

rows.under: Portrays an image of never being wrong. Hides the miss or blames the weather.
rows.justRight: Takes responsibility for what they or the team did not deliver, names the cause, and says what changes.
rows.over: Is so self-deprecating that it reads as a lack of confidence, or as a performance.

rows.under: Defends the team past the point of honesty, or refuses to accept any responsibility.
rows.justRight: Owns the miss upward without naming individuals as the problem. Gives the team the real feedback in private.
rows.over: Throws the team under the bus to protect a personal reputation.

rows.situation: When a problem is still small
rows.under: Covers the problem and discourages sharing. Blind spots grow, and the same error repeats.
rows.justRight: Is honest about team performance. Surfaces the real shortfall while it is still cheap to fix.
rows.over: Is self-critical about trivia, or dwells until morale and confidence collapse.

rows.under: Does not listen. Talks over critics. Treats disagreement as disloyalty.
rows.justRight: Listens all the way through, speaks candidly, and changes the plan when the other person is right.
rows.over: Agrees with everyone in the room so nobody is upset, and the decision is mush.

rows.under: Arrogant and disrespectful. Builds walls. Questions motives instead of the work.
rows.justRight: Treats peers as colleagues on the same customer problem. Uses data to settle the conflict and gives credit when another team carried it.
rows.over: Spends the week on lunches and relationship theater, and the deliverable slips.

rows.under: Makes a soft promise, hedges, or stays vague so nobody can say they missed.
rows.justRight: Makes a hard, clear promise and keeps it. If they cannot keep it, they say so early and repair it.
rows.over: Promises anything to be liked, then burns trust when the thing does not arrive.

rows.under: Hides behind another team, a system, or an act of God.
rows.justRight: Calls it like it is, on their team or someone else's. Names the miss, names the fix, and moves.
rows.over: Takes blame they do not own in order to keep a relationship, and the root cause stays unfixed.

rows.situation: When comparing the team to the best
rows.under: Assumes the team is already the best. Unapproachable. No intensity on getting better.
rows.justRight: Benchmarks against the best, shows the gap, and stays approachable enough that people will bring the next gap to them.
rows.over: Publishes only the failures. Other teams start to doubt the group can {lp:deliver-results}.

rows.situation: When the team needs the truth
rows.under: Accepts that the team failed and then blames the people below. Avoids the hard conversation.
rows.justRight: Owns the problem as the leader, seeks the pain points, and still gives clear, tough feedback with a standard attached.
rows.over: Protects the team from every hard word, or points out every fault until nobody will take a risk.

rows.situation: When it would be easy to be clever
rows.under: Wins the room by being clever at someone else's expense. Escalates past a person they have not spoken to.
rows.justRight: Is kind without being soft. Talks to the person first. Optimizes for the customer and the company, not a personal scoreboard.
rows.over: Makes being liked the goal. Will not risk a relationship even when the customer is losing.

examples.title: Make a hard promise and keep it
examples.body: You tell a customer exactly when the thing will arrive, and at what price. That promise is expensive to make. You keep it. The next time you launch into a new category, they try it because the last promise held. Soft promises feel safer. They do not earn trust.

examples.title: Lead with the miss
examples.body: In the review, the leader opens with what did not work, what they got wrong, and what they will change. They do not open with the highlight reel. People in the room start telling the truth about their own work. That is the point of being vocally self-critical. It is not a confession contest.

examples.title: Own it up, coach it down
examples.body: A process change ships too wide, and customers start getting the wrong thing. The leader who made the change says so, names the root cause, and puts a smaller-batch control in place before the next launch. They do not brief the miss as a story about an individual on the team. The individual still gets the real note, in private.

looksLike.individual: An individual who earns trust is on time, says the uncomfortable true thing, and does not need a witness to keep a commitment. They admit the mistake while it is still cheap. They do not gossip about motives. They give credit in the room where it would have been easy to keep it.
looksLike.manager: A manager who earns trust is vocally self-critical about their own calls, never about a person on the team in a public setting. They keep hard promises to other teams. They listen to critics. They benchmark against the best, not against last year. People bring them bad news early because the last person who did was not punished for it.

deepen: What hard promise did you make recently, and did you keep it?
When was the last time you led with a miss in a room that could have punished you for it?
Whose credit did you give away in public this month, and whose miss did you take in public?
If I asked your critics what you do when you are wrong, what would they say?
Where are you still performing competence instead of asking for help?
When someone told you that you broke trust, what did you do in the first day after that conversation?
Are you kind, or are you clever at someone else's expense?
What team do you benchmark against, and where do you still smell like roses?
Do people bring you bad news early, or do they wait until it is a crisis?
When you brief a miss upward, do you name a person, or do you name a cause and a fix?

related.note: You cannot earn trust while you let defects walk past you. Standards without humility is arrogance.
Candor without backbone is agreeable. Backbone without respect is a fight. Trust needs both.
People develop when they trust the feedback and the person giving it.
Being right a lot requires other people to tell you when you are wrong. They will not, if they do not trust you.
Publishing only the failures makes other teams doubt you can deliver. Trust includes a track record.
